pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Thallium Poisoning (Acute Thallotoxicosis) THE SMOKING GUN: The triad of severe, painful ascending peripheral neuropathy, gastrointestinal distress, and acute diffuse alopecia (hair loss) appearing 2 to 3 weeks after exposure, alongside Mees' lines on the nails. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Thallium is a potent, heavy-metal toxin that acts as a cellular poison. Due to its ionic radius being nearly identical to that of potassium, the body mistakenly imports thallium via Na+/K+-ATPase pumps. Once intracellular, thallium disrupts cellular energy production by inhibiting critical enzymes in the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. It binds strongly to sulfhydryl groups on proteins, leading to widespread cellular death. This results in severe axonal degeneration of peripheral nerves (causing intense pain and motor paralysis), autonomic nervous system dysfunction, central nervous system toxicity (hallucinations and psychosis), and necrosis of hair follicle cells leading to characteristic rapid-onset alopecia.
